probes.name: Non-Being
probes.description: Absolute absence, the void, nothing.
support_texts: Non-being is the absence of all existence.
Nothing exists in the void.
The concept of nothing is paradoxical - to conceive nothing is to conceive something.
Ex nihilo nihil fit - from nothing, nothing comes.
Parmenides: Non-being cannot be thought.

probes.name: Potential
probes.description: That which can be but is not yet - potentiality, dynamis.
support_texts: Potential is the capacity to become actual.
Aristotle's dynamis: the power to change or be changed.
The seed is potentially a tree.
Potentiality is being-in-waiting.
Matter is pure potentiality.

probes.name: Becoming
probes.description: The process of change - genesis, transition.
support_texts: Becoming is the passage from potential to actual.
Heraclitus: Everything flows, nothing stands still.
Becoming is being that is not yet complete.
Process philosophy: Reality is fundamentally becoming.
Change is the actualization of the potential qua potential.

probes.name: Actual
probes.description: That which exists in fact - actuality, energeia.
support_texts: The actual is what exists in reality, not merely in thought.
Aristotle's energeia: being-at-work, activity.
Actuality is prior to potentiality.
The actual is the real as opposed to the merely possible.
Existence precedes essence - Sartre.

probes.name: Substance
probes.description: That which exists in itself - ousia, substratum.
support_texts: Substance is that which exists independently.
Aristotle: Substance is the primary sense of being.
Substance is the bearer of attributes.
Spinoza: God or Nature is the one substance.
That which remains constant through change.

probes.name: Necessary Being
probes.description: That which cannot not exist - ens necessarium.
support_texts: Necessary being exists by its own nature.
That which exists in all possible worlds.
God is the necessary being - Aquinas.
The uncaused cause, the unmoved mover.
Self-existent being requires no explanation.

probes.name: Ignorance
probes.description: The absence of knowledge - agnoia.
support_texts: Ignorance is the absence of knowledge.
Socrates: I know that I know nothing.
Ignorance can be simple (not knowing) or vincible (culpable).
The first step to wisdom is knowing your ignorance.
Docta ignorantia - learned ignorance.

probes.name: Opinion
probes.description: Belief without certainty - doxa.
support_texts: Opinion is belief that may or may not be true.
Plato: Opinion is between knowledge and ignorance.
Doxa is the realm of appearance, not reality.
Opinion can be true or false, right or wrong.
Common opinion is often mistaken.

probes.name: Belief
probes.description: Acceptance of a proposition as true.
support_texts: Belief is holding something to be true.
Belief may or may not be justified.
True belief is not yet knowledge.
Belief is a propositional attitude.
We believe what we cannot prove.

probes.name: Understanding
probes.description: Grasping the reason why - episteme.
support_texts: Understanding is knowing why, not merely that.
Aristotle: Scientific knowledge is knowledge of causes.
Understanding grasps necessary connections.
To understand is to see the reason.
Comprehension of the whole from the parts.

probes.name: Knowledge
probes.description: Justified true belief - episteme, scientia.
support_texts: Knowledge is justified true belief.
Plato: Knowledge is opinion plus logos.
Knowledge requires truth, belief, and justification.
We know what we can demonstrate.
Knowledge is certain, opinion uncertain.

probes.name: Wisdom
probes.description: Knowledge of first principles and causes - sophia.
support_texts: Wisdom is knowledge of ultimate things.
Aristotle: Wisdom is knowledge of first causes.
Sophia is the highest form of knowledge.
Wisdom combines theoretical and practical knowledge.
Philosophy is the love of wisdom.

probes.name: Impossibility
probes.description: That which cannot be - logical impossibility.
support_texts: The impossible cannot exist in any possible world.
Round squares are impossible.
Logical impossibility: self-contradictory.
What is impossible is necessarily not the case.
Impossibility is the negation of all possibility.

probes.name: Possibility
probes.description: That which can be - logical possibility.
support_texts: The possible is that which is not self-contradictory.
Possible worlds: ways things could have been.
Logical possibility is broader than physical possibility.
What is possible may or may not be actual.
Possibility is the ground of becoming.

probes.name: Contingent Being
probes.description: That which exists but might not have - contingent existence.
support_texts: Contingent beings depend on something else for their existence.
I exist, but I might not have existed.
Contingent beings require a cause.
The world is contingent - it might not have existed.
Contingency implies dependence.

probes.name: Actuality
probes.description: That which is the case - the actual world.
support_texts: The actual world is one among many possible worlds.
Actuality is the realized possibility.
What is actual is possible, but not vice versa.
The actual world is indexically given.
Actuality selects among possibilities.

probes.name: Necessity
probes.description: That which must be - necessary existence.
support_texts: Necessary truths hold in all possible worlds.
Necessary beings cannot fail to exist.
Mathematical truths are necessary.
What is necessary cannot be otherwise.
Necessity is the denial of all contingency.

probes.name: Absolute
probes.description: That which is unconditional and self-sufficient.
support_texts: The Absolute is that which depends on nothing else.
Hegel: The Absolute is the whole, the truth.
The Absolute is being-in-itself-and-for-itself.
Unconditioned by any external factor.
The Absolute is the ground of all that is.

probes.name: Plurality
probes.description: The many - multiplicity, diversity.
support_texts: Plurality is the existence of many distinct things.
The many versus the one.
Multiplicity is the opposite of unity.
Plurality presupposes distinction.
The many are held together by the one.

probes.name: Part
probes.description: A component of a whole - meros.
support_texts: A part is less than the whole.
Parts are proper parts if not identical to the whole.
Every whole has parts (atomism excepted).
The part depends on the whole for its nature.
Parthood is transitive: part of part is part of whole.

probes.name: Aggregate
probes.description: A collection without essential unity.
support_texts: An aggregate is parts together without forming a true whole.
A heap is an aggregate, not a unity.
Aggregates lack organic unity.
The aggregate is the sum of its parts, nothing more.
Mere collection versus true composition.

probes.name: Whole
probes.description: That which contains parts as a unity - holon.
support_texts: The whole is more than the sum of its parts.
A true whole has organic unity.
The whole determines the nature of the parts.
Holism: the whole is prior to the parts.
The whole is one, the parts are many.

probes.name: Composition
probes.description: The combining of parts into a whole.
support_texts: Composition is the relation between parts and whole.
When do parts compose a whole? (The special composition question.)
Composition is identity - the whole is nothing over and above its parts.
Material constitution versus identity.
The composite is made of its components.

probes.name: Unity
probes.description: Oneness, the absence of division - to hen.
support_texts: Unity is the principle that makes something one.
Plotinus: The One is beyond being.
Unity is prior to plurality.
The simple is absolutely one, without parts.
Being and unity are convertible (ens et unum convertuntur).

probes.name: philosophy
probes.description: Etymology: philosophia (greek), love of wisdom; shift: From love of wisdom to academic discipline
support_texts: The word 'philosophy' comes from greek 'philosophia', meaning 'love of wisdom'.
'philosophy' originally meant 'love of wisdom' but now refers to something broader.
When we use 'philosophy', we echo its greek roots in 'philosophia'.
The concept of philosophy evolved from love of wisdom to its modern meaning.

probes.name: logic
probes.description: Etymology: logike (greek), the art of reasoning; shift: From reasoning art to formal symbolic system
support_texts: The word 'logic' comes from greek 'logike', meaning 'the art of reasoning'.
'logic' originally meant 'the art of reasoning' but now refers to something broader.
When we use 'logic', we echo its greek roots in 'logike'.
The concept of logic evolved from the art of reasoning to its modern meaning.

probes.name: ethics
probes.description: Etymology: ethikos (greek), relating to character; shift: From character study to moral philosophy
support_texts: The word 'ethics' comes from greek 'ethikos', meaning 'relating to character'.
'ethics' originally meant 'relating to character' but now refers to something broader.
When we use 'ethics', we echo its greek roots in 'ethikos'.
The concept of ethics evolved from relating to character to its modern meaning.

probes.name: metaphysics
probes.description: Etymology: ta meta ta physika (greek), the things after physics; shift: From book ordering to study of reality beyond physics
support_texts: The word 'metaphysics' comes from greek 'ta meta ta physika', meaning 'the things after physics'.
'metaphysics' originally meant 'the things after physics' but now refers to something broader.
When we use 'metaphysics', we echo its greek roots in 'ta meta ta physika'.
The concept of metaphysics evolved from the things after physics to its modern meaning.

probes.name: ontology
probes.description: Etymology: ontos + logos (greek), study of being; shift: From being-study to existence taxonomy
support_texts: The word 'ontology' comes from greek 'ontos + logos', meaning 'study of being'.
'ontology' originally meant 'study of being' but now refers to something broader.
When we use 'ontology', we echo its greek roots in 'ontos + logos'.
The concept of ontology evolved from study of being to its modern meaning.

probes.name: natural philosophy -> physics
probes.description: Lineage: natural philosophy evolved_into physics
support_texts: Natural philosophy became modern physics.

probes.name: alchemy -> chemistry
probes.description: Lineage: alchemy evolved_into chemistry
support_texts: Alchemy transformed into the science of chemistry.

probes.name: rhetoric -> communication studies
probes.description: Lineage: rhetoric evolved_into communication studies
support_texts: Classical rhetoric evolved into communication studies.

probes.name: logic -> computer science
probes.description: Lineage: logic influenced computer science
support_texts: Aristotelian logic influenced the foundations of computer science.
